CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY & PRESCRIBING__Saf:
Overview — Safe Prescribing & Prescribing Errors
The practical/clinical-governance counterpart to the prescribing-safety cluster: how to prescribe safely and why errors happen + how to prevent them.
The guiding philosophy: errors are usually a systems failure, not individual incompetence — the safe-prescribing response is to fix the system, not just blame the person.
Two halves: the principles of good prescribing (proactive) and the anatomy of prescribing errors (what goes wrong + prevention). Cross-ref: PK/PD, ADRs/Yellow Card, renal/hepatic dose adjustment, drugs in pregnancy, anticoagulation/insulin/steroids.
The Principles of Good Prescribing
Before prescribing, work through the core principles of good prescribing:
  • Clarify the indication — is a drug actually needed?
  • Take a full drug history — current + recent meds, incl. OTC + herbal; medication reconciliation
  • Check allergies + prior ADRs — avoid recurrence
  • Consider patient factors — age, pregnancy, renal/hepatic/cardiac function, genetics, comorbidity
  • Check interactions — you can't know them all → look them up (BNF)
  • Choose effective, safe, cost-effective drugs — right drug, dose, route, frequency, duration
  • Share the decision — patient ideas/concerns/expectations, informed consent
  • Write the prescription clearly (legible, generic names, no dangerous abbreviations)
  • Monitor + review — efficacy, ADRs, when to stop; deprescribe where appropriate
Use generic (non-proprietary) names — reduces confusion + reconciliation errors.
Writing a Safe Prescription
📷 Image placeholder — Correctly written drug-chart entry — generic name in CAPITALS, “micrograms”/“units” in full, no trailing zero, leading zero (0.5 not .5), with route/frequency/allergy box — beside common dangerous-abbreviation errors
The dangerous-abbreviation rules (high-yield / PSA)
  • Write "micrograms"/"nanograms" in full — never "mcg"/"µg" (misread as mg)
  • Write "units" in full — never "U" (misread as a zero → 10× insulin overdose)
  • No trailing zeros ("2 mg" not "2.0 mg"). Doses of 1 g or more in grams; under 1 g in milligrams (500 mg, not 0.5 g); under 1 mg in micrograms (500 micrograms, not 0.5 mg). Use a decimal point only where unavoidable, and then with a leading zero ("0.5 mL" not ".5 mL")
  • Legible, in ink, signed + dated; generic name in CAPITALS
  • Route, frequency, duration/quantity; max dose for PRN; allergy status documented
  • Controlled drugs: additional legal requirements — the form; the strength where more than one exists; the dose (clearly specified, but it need not be in words and figures); and the total quantity or number of dosage units in both words and figures. Valid for 28 days from the date on the prescription
Classifying Prescribing Errors

Stage Example error

By psychology (Reason's taxonomy)
Type Definition
MistakeWrong plan (knowledge/rule-based) — e.g. prescribing the wrong drug for the condition
SlipRight plan, wrong action (attention failure) — e.g. writing the wrong dose by accident
LapseMemory failure — e.g. forgetting to prescribe a needed drug
ViolationDeliberate deviation from a known rule — strictly not an error, since the act is intended, though the harm is not
High-Risk Medications
"A PINCH" (an Australian mnemonic — there is no equivalent UK acronym) — the drugs causing disproportionate harm: Anti-infectives, Potassium and other electrolytes, Insulin, Narcotics (opioids) and other sedatives, Chemotherapy, Heparin and other anticoagulants (+ sedatives).
  • Insulin ("U" misread → 10× dose)
  • Anticoagulants (warfarin/heparin → bleeding)
  • Opioids (respiratory depression)
  • Methotrexate — weekly not daily (a classic fatal error): prescribe one strength only (2.5 mg tablets), specify the day of the week, folic acid on a different day, with FBC, LFTs and U&Es monitored
  • Potassium — never as an IV bolus: give it diluted by infusion, not normally faster than 10 mmol/hour or above 40 mmol/L peripherally, using pre-mixed bags — never made up on the ward (cross-ref electrolytes)
  • Gentamicin/vancomycin — need TDM
These need extra checks, monitoring, and often double-checking (e.g. insulin, chemo).
Why Errors Happen — the Systems Approach
The Swiss cheese model (Reason): errors result from multiple latent system failures lining up, not a single person's mistake — defences have "holes" that occasionally align.
  • Contributing factors: inadequate knowledge/training, an incomplete drug history, poor communication/handover, fatigue + workload (on-call prescribing), look-alike/sound-alike drugs, trade names, distraction
  • A "just culture": honest error is treated as a system problem — focus on what went wrong, not who — so that staff report and learn rather than conceal. It is not a blanket "no-blame" culture: recklessness and deliberate violations still carry individual accountability
Preventing Errors — system-level safeguards
Medication reconciliation — a core defence at transitions of care
Especially at admission/discharge transitions. Three steps: verify (accurate drug history) → clarify (appropriate drugs/doses) → reconcile (document changes). (NICE) recommends it within 24 hours of admission to an acute setting, or sooner if clinically necessary. It is most reliable when pharmacist-led.
  • Medication review + deprescribing (esp. polypharmacy/elderly — STOPP/START — the tool generally used in the UK — and, from US practice, the Beers criteria — for inappropriate prescribing in the elderly)
  • Electronic prescribing (ePMA) with decision support (interaction/allergy/dose alerts)
  • Double-checking high-risk drugs; standardised processes; BNF/protocols
  • Reporting + learning: local incident reporting (e.g. Datix), which feeds the national Learn from Patient Safety Events service; the Yellow Card scheme for suspected ADRs; and Never Events (e.g. wrong-route chemo, insulin overdose from an abbreviation, methotrexate overdose in non-cancer treatment) — wholly preventable patient safety incidents for which strong national barriers already exist. These are different systems: incident reporting records patient safety events, while the Yellow Card scheme reports suspected adverse drug reactions to the MHRA — one event may need both

Overview — ADRs & Yellow Card
📷 Image placeholder — Yellow Card thresholds — black-triangle ▼ drugs/vaccines/biosimilars: report ALL suspected reactions; established drugs: report all SERIOUS reactions (plus all in children and pregnancy)
ADR = a noxious + unintended response to a drug at normal therapeutic doses — distinct from overdose/toxicity, and from medication errors.
Two organising frameworks
  • How do we classify ADRs? — Rawlins-Thompson A–E
  • How do we report them? — the Yellow Card scheme
Cross-ref: PK/PD & drug interactions (mechanisms — this note's parent topic), toxicology (overdose — distinct from ADR), safe prescribing, hypersensitivity (type B immune ADRs), anaphylaxis (the emergency management and adrenaline dose).
Definitions — get the distinctions straight
  • ADR = harmful, unintended response at normal doses (≠ overdose)
  • Side effect = a known, often predictable secondary effect (a subset of ADRs)
  • Adverse drug event = any harm associated with a drug, including from medication error (broader)
Serious ADR (MHRA definition): one that is fatal, life-threatening, disabling/incapacitating, causes/prolongs hospitalisation, causes a congenital abnormality, or is otherwise medically significant.
The Rawlins-Thompson Classification (A–E)
📷 Image placeholder — Rawlins-Thompson types — A augmented/dose-related (usually dose-adjust), B bizarre/immune (STOP + avoid), C chronic, D delayed, E end-of-use/withdrawal (+ F failure)
Type Name Features Examples
AAugmented (commonest)Dose-dependent, predictable, exaggeration of the drug's action; low case-fatality per reaction, but so common that Type A causes most ADR admissions and deathsβ-blocker → bradycardia; opioid → resp depression; insulin → hypoglycaemia; anticoagulant → bleeding
BBizarre (2nd commonest)NOT dose-dependent, unpredictable, often immune-mediated; high mortalityPenicillin anaphylaxis, malignant hyperthermia, carbamazepine → SJS, Reye's (aspirin)
CChronic/ContinuedDose + time-dependent, with prolonged useSteroids → osteoporosis, bisphosphonates → osteonecrosis of jaw
DDelayedAppears long after exposureTeratogenesis (thalidomide), carcinogenesis, tardive dyskinesia
EEnd-of-use (withdrawal)On stopping (esp. abrupt)Steroid withdrawal → adrenal crisis, benzodiazepine/opioid withdrawal, β-blocker rebound
Mnemonic — ABCDE: Augmented, Bizarre, Chronic, Delayed, End-of-use. (Some add F = Failure of therapy — e.g. reduced efficacy from a drug interaction.)
The key split: Type A = predictable + dose-dependent (the bulk — reduce the dose if mild, but stop the drug and treat actively if severe: opioid respiratory depression, major bleeding, severe hypoglycaemia); Type B = unpredictable + immune (stop the drug, avoid it and cross-reacting drugs permanently, and document it as an allergy — cross-ref hypersensitivity).
Risk Factors for ADRs
  • Extremes of age (elderly + neonates — altered PK)
  • Polypharmacy (interaction risk)
  • Organ impairment (renal/hepatic — cross-ref dose adjustment)
  • Female sex
  • Genetic factors (CYP polymorphisms, G6PD)
  • Multiple comorbidities
Recognising & Assessing an ADR
  • Causality assessment: temporal relationship to starting the drug, known reaction profile, improvement on stopping (dechallenge) and recurrence on restarting (rechallenge), exclusion of other causes; formalised by scales (Naranjo). Rechallenge is usually only observed inadvertently — deliberate rechallenge is contraindicated after any serious or Type B reaction (anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN, DRESS, agranulocytosis are never re-exposed)
  • High-yield "classic culprits": ACE inhibitors → dry cough (benign — switch to an ARB) and angioedema (airway emergency: stop permanently, never restart, and it can appear months or years into treatment), statins → myopathy, amiodarone → multi-organ, methotrexate → marrow/liver (and methotrexate is dosed once weekly, never daily) (and the drugs flagged across the DILI / anticoagulation / steroid notes)
The Yellow Card Scheme
Run by the MHRA (+ Commission on Human Medicines) — the UK system for post-marketing pharmacovigilance (drug-safety surveillance after licensing). Clinical trials are too small/short to detect rare or delayed ADRs → real-world reporting detects new safety signals.
  • Who can report: anyone — doctors, pharmacists, nurses, and patients/carers (voluntary; no proof of causation needed — report on suspicion)
Always report Detail
ALL suspected ADRs to "black triangle" (▼) drugsNew drugs/vaccines under additional monitoring — report any reaction, however minor
ALL serious suspected ADRs to established drugsEven if the reaction is already well-recognised
ALL suspected ADRs in children (<18)Even if the drug is off-label
Suspected ADRs in pregnancyHowever minor
Delayed reactions (cancers, fibrosis)Even years later
What's reportable: reactions to any therapeutic agent — prescribed and OTC/self-medication, vaccines, blood products, radiographic contrast, herbal/complementary and homeopathic products — and also medical devices (including software and apps), defective medicines (not of acceptable quality), falsified (fake) medicines and devices, and e-cigarettes and e-liquids.
How: online via the MHRA Yellow Card website, the Yellow Card app, via clinical IT systems, or by post on a freepost Yellow Card form.
For reporting purposes the MHRA also wants suspected reactions arising from medication error, overdose, misuse, abuse and off-label or unlicensed use — the reporting threshold is wider than the classroom definition of an ADR.
The black triangle (▼): marks medicines under additional monitoring — newly-licensed drugs and vaccines, all new biologicals including biosimilars, and medicines with conditions attached to their licence; appears in the BNF + SmPC/PIL → report all reactions to these.
Minimising ADRs — the prescribing-safety link
  • Take a full drug + allergy history (incl. OTC/herbal)
  • Avoid polypharmacy (deprescribe); check interactions (BNF)
  • Start low, go slow in the elderly/organ impairment; use the fewest drugs
  • Monitor high-risk drugs; document + communicate allergies/reactions
  • Medication reconciliation at transitions of care (cross-ref safe prescribing)

Overview — Pain Management & Analgesia
The framework for analgesic prescribing: assess the pain → classify it → treat by the WHO ladder + by mechanism → prescribe opioids safely.
Classification 1 — Acute vs Chronic
Chronic = >3 months.
Classification 2 — Nociceptive vs Neuropathic
Different drugs — opioids work poorly on neuropathic pain.
Cross-ref: palliative care (palliative-specific opioid dosing/conversion/syringe drivers live there — this is the general framework), toxicology (opioid overdose → naloxone), PK/PD (opioid metabolism), MSK/neurology (chronic pain conditions).
Pain Assessment
  • Pain is subjective — measured by the patient's report: Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) and Numerical Rating Scale (NRS, 0–10)
  • SOCRATES for characterising pain; DN4 questionnaire (≥4/10 → neuropathic)
  • Assess impact (function, sleep, mood) — pain is biopsychosocial
Classifying Pain — directs the treatment
Type Mechanism Character Responds to
NociceptiveTissue damage → nociceptor activationAching, throbbing, well-localisedWHO ladder (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids)
NeuropathicNerve damage/dysfunctionBurning, shooting, tingling, allodyniaNeuropathic agents (opioids work poorly)
AcuteRecent, protective, self-limiting—Treat the cause + WHO ladder
Chronic>3 months—Multimodal; chronic primary pain → avoid most analgesia
The WHO Analgesic Ladder
📷 Image placeholder — WHO analgesic ladder — Step 1 non-opioid (paracetamol ± NSAID), Step 2 weak opioid (codeine/tramadol), Step 3 strong opioid (morphine/oxycodone/fentanyl), ± adjuvant at every step
Originally for cancer pain, now applied to acute + chronic pain; step up until pain controlled.
Step Pain Drugs
1MildNon-opioid: paracetamol 1 g QDS (max 4 g/24 h) ± NSAID — ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food (max 2.4 g/24 h) or naproxen 250–500 mg BD with food (max 1 g/24 h) (± adjuvant)
2ModerateWeak opioid: codeine 30–60 mg 4-hourly PRN (max 240 mg/24 h), dihydrocodeine 30 mg 4–6-hourly PRN (max 180 mg/24 h), or tramadol 50–100 mg 4–6-hourly PRN (max 400 mg/24 h) (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
3SevereStrong opioid: morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl. In the opioid-naive start modified-release morphine 10 mg BD (or immediate-release 5 mg 4-hourly), with immediate-release morphine 5 mg PRN for breakthrough (+ non-opioid ± adjuvant)
The principles — "by the mouth, by the clock, by the ladder, for the individual": oral route preferred, regular dosing (not just PRN) for continuous pain, step-wise, individualised. Leapfrogging allowed — severe pain → start at Step 3 directly; breakthrough pain → a fast-acting rescue dose of immediate-release morphine, one sixth of the total 24-hour oral morphine dose (so 5 mg if the total is 30 mg/24 h).
Step 4 (modern addition): interventional — nerve blocks, spinal analgesia, spinal cord stimulation.
The opioid-crisis caveat: the ladder drove opioid overuse in chronic non-cancer pain; weak opioids (Step 2) add little and modern practice questions them.
The Analgesics by Class
Drug/class Mechanism Key cautions
ParacetamolCentral (poorly understood)Hepatotoxic in overdose (cross-ref toxicology); dose-reduce in liver disease and at low body weight — if under 50 kg, reduce to 500 mg every 4–6 hours
NSAIDsInhibit COX → ↓prostaglandinsGI ulcer/bleed, renal impairment, CVD, asthma; avoid in CKD/PUD/heart failure; co-prescribe a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg OD, or lansoprazole 30 mg OD) for as long as the NSAID continues, and use the lowest effective dose for the shortest period
Weak opioids (codeine, tramadol)µ-opioid agonist; codeine is a prodrug → morphine (CYP2D6)Codeine ineffective in poor metabolisers, dangerous in ultra-rapid metabolisers — hence contraindicated under 12 years, in breastfeeding, and in under-18s after tonsillectomy/adenoidectomy for sleep apnoea (MHRA); tramadol 50–100 mg 4–6-hourly PRN, max 400 mg/24 h — it also lowers the seizure threshold and is serotonergic
Strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl)µ-opioid agonistSee opioid section below
Opioid Prescribing & Safety
ALWAYS co-prescribe a laxative — senna 15 mg at night (± docusate 100 mg BD if stools are hard) — constipation is near-universal; consider a PRN antiemetic when starting, such as metoclopramide 10 mg up to TDS (max 5 days — MHRA) or cyclizine 50 mg up to TDS.
  • Side effects: constipation (near-universal), nausea (often transient), drowsiness (mild sedation on starting or increasing a dose is expected and usually settles within a few days — persistent or worsening drowsiness with confusion is toxicity), respiratory depression, pruritus, tolerance + dependence
  • Opioid toxicity: drowsiness → confusion, pinpoint pupils, myoclonus, respiratory depression → reduce dose / rotate opioid; naloxone only if life-threatening (cross-ref toxicology)
  • Renal impairment: morphine accumulates (active metabolites) → use oxycodone (still at a reduced dose), or fentanyl/buprenorphine (cross-ref renal dose adjustment)
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)
IV strong opioid, patient-triggered, locked to prevent overdose; needs anaesthetic input + naloxone/antiemetic/atropine available; avoid other PRN opioids alongside.
Opioid patches (background analgesia)
Buprenorphine, fentanyl — for stable chronic pain, not acute titration. Never start a fentanyl patch in an opioid-naive patient, and warn that heat — fever, a hot bath, a heat pad — increases absorption (MHRA).
Palliative-specific dosing (breakthrough = 1/6 of the total 24-hour dose, oral→SC conversions) lives in the palliative care note.
Neuropathic Pain — different drugs
📷 Image placeholder — NICE neuropathic pain first-line — one of amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin or pregabalin; switch if one fails; carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia
Opioids work poorly — use specific agents. NICE first-line (choose one of four): amitriptyline 10 mg at night, increased in 10 mg steps to 25–75 mg at night; duloxetine 60 mg OD; gabapentin 300 mg OD increasing over 3 days to TDS, then in 300 mg steps to a maximum of 3.6 g/24 h; or pregabalin 75 mg BD, increased to a maximum of 600 mg/24 h (switch if one fails). Gabapentin and pregabalin are Schedule 3 controlled drugs — dependence and misuse risk, taper on stopping, and there is an MHRA warning on respiratory depression in the elderly, in respiratory compromise and with opioids; avoid pregabalin in pregnancy unless clearly necessary, with effective contraception advised (MHRA).
  • Tramadol as rescue only; capsaicin cream for localised; carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia specifically — 100 mg once or twice daily, increased in 100–200 mg steps until the pain is controlled
  • Causes: diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia, nerve impingement, MS, trigeminal neuralgia
Adjuvants
Drugs not primarily analgesic but useful in specific pain:
  • Antidepressants (amitriptyline, duloxetine — neuropathic)
  • Anticonvulsants (gabapentin/pregabalin — neuropathic)
  • Corticosteroids (inflammatory / nerve compression / raised ICP)
  • Bisphosphonates (bone pain)
  • Benzodiazepines (muscle spasm), antispasmodics
Chronic Pain Principles — the NICE exam point
Chronic primary pain (no underlying cause — e.g. fibromyalgia): NICE recommends avoiding most analgesia (paracetamol/NSAIDs/opioids/gabapentinoids) → instead exercise, psychological therapy (CBT/ACT), and consider an antidepressant (e.g. duloxetine or amitriptyline) — the high-yield SBA.
  • Chronic secondary pain (underlying cause): treat the cause + multimodal analgesia
  • Multimodal/biopsychosocial: physiotherapy, psychology, pain clinic; minimise long-term opioids (limited benefit + harms in chronic non-cancer pain)
Specific Contexts
  • Post-operative: regular paracetamol + NSAID + PRN IMMEDIATE-RELEASE opioid — modified-release opioids are not used for acute post-operative pain (they cannot be titrated against a rapidly falling requirement, they accumulate in the opioid-naive, and they drive persistent post-surgical opioid use); step the opioid down daily; local anaesthetic wound infiltration; PCA; reduce as recovering
  • Acute severe pain: titrated IV opioid — morphine 1–2 mg IV repeated every 5 minutes, titrated to pain and respiratory rate

Overview — Renal / Hepatic Dose Adjustment Principles
📷 Image placeholder — Child-Pugh score — the 5 components (bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy) and A/B/C grading
The kidneys and liver are the two main routes of drug elimination — kidney = excretion (water-soluble drugs + metabolites), liver = metabolism. Impair either and drugs/active metabolites accumulate → toxicity.
Two decisive questions for any drug in organ impairment
  • How is it cleared — renal vs hepatic?
  • How narrow is its therapeutic window?
Together these determine whether dose adjustment matters.
A principles note — the BNF's renal and hepatic impairment guidance and the individual drug monographs hold the per-drug detail; the examinable skill is the reasoning + recognising the classic dangerous drugs. Cross-ref: AKI/CKD, DILI, anticoagulation, PK/PD, toxicology.
Pharmacokinetic Framework — the ADME lens
ADME step Affected by Consequence
AbsorptionGut oedema, altered first-passVariable bioavailability
Distribution↓albumin (liver/nephrotic)More free (active) drug for protein-bound drugs
MetabolismLiver impairment↓clearance of hepatically-metabolised drugs
ExcretionKidney impairment↓clearance of renally-excreted drugs
The core mechanism: impairment → ↓clearance → ↑plasma level + prolonged half-life → accumulation → toxicity, unless dose/interval is adjusted.
Renal Dose Adjustment
📷 Image placeholder — DOAC renal thresholds — apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban (avoid <15) vs dabigatran (contraindicated <30) by CrCl
  • Who's at risk: drugs that are renally excreted (especially unchanged), have active renally-cleared metabolites, and/or a narrow therapeutic index
  • How you adjust: reduce the dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval; some drugs are contraindicated below a certain eGFR
Assessing function for dosing: eGFR is the usual measure, but DOACs, aminoglycosides and digoxin must be dosed on creatinine clearance (Cockcroft-Gault), not eGFR — eGFR is normalised to a body surface area of 1.73 m² and CrCl is not, so in small, elderly or very obese patients eGFR overstates true clearance and leads to overdosing. eGFR is also unreliable in AKI (not at steady state) and at extremes of body habitus.
Drug Why / what happens
Aminoglycosides (gentamicin)Nephrotoxic + ototoxic; renally cleared → monitor levels (once-daily regimens: level 6–14 h after the first dose; multiple-daily regimens: after 3–4 doses — check earlier and more often in renal impairment)
VancomycinNephrotoxic, narrow window → TDM
MetforminAccumulates → lactic acidosis. Review the dose at eGFR 30–44 (max 1 g/day; do not start below 45); stop at eGFR <30 and in AKI; withhold during any acute dehydrating illness
LithiumNarrow window → toxicity → TDM
DigoxinNarrow window → toxicity → TDM
DOACs / LMWHAccumulate → bleeding. All DOAC thresholds are CrCl, not eGFR: apixaban avoid if CrCl <15, and in AF reduce to 2.5 mg BD if CrCl 15–29 or if two of (age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥133 micromol/L); rivaroxaban 15 mg OD if CrCl 15–49, avoid <15; edoxaban 30 mg OD if CrCl 15–50, avoid <15; dabigatran contraindicated if CrCl <30. LMWH accumulates from CrCl <30 — reduce the treatment dose (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg once daily) or switch to unfractionated heparin
Opioids — morphineActive renally-excreted metabolite accumulates → toxicity. Use oxycodone at a reduced dose in mild–moderate impairment; in severe impairment (eGFR <30) oxycodone also accumulates — use alfentanil, fentanyl or buprenorphine
NitrofurantoinNeeds renal secretion into urine to work, and accumulates systemically → neuropathy. Avoid if eGFR <45; a short 3–7 day course may be used with caution at eGFR 30–44 if benefit outweighs risk
Gabapentin / pregabalinAlmost entirely renally cleared with no hepatic metabolism → accumulate → sedation and respiratory depression; reduce the dose by CrCl band
Methotrexate, allopurinol, many antibioticsRenally cleared → reduce/avoid
Drugs to withhold in AKI — "AADN": ACEi/ARB, Aminoglycosides, Diuretics, NSAIDs (cross-ref AKI); the commonly used UK sick-day version is DAMN — Diuretics, ACEi/ARB, Metformin, NSAIDs (add SGLT2 inhibitors). Only aminoglycosides and NSAIDs are directly nephrotoxic; ACEi/ARB and diuretics are not — they impair renal perfusion and autoregulation, so they are withheld during the acute illness and restarted on recovery, not stopped for good. The "may need to stop" list (metformin, lithium, digoxin) also applies — these accumulate rather than damage the kidney. Sick-day rule: withhold these prospectively during any vomiting, diarrhoea or fever illness and restart after 24–48 h of normal eating and drinking.
Hepatic Dose Adjustment — the trickier one
Why it's harder than renal: there's no "eGFR for the liver" — use clinical severity (Child-Pugh), LFTs, and synthetic function (albumin, INR, bilirubin) as a guide, rather than a clean number to dose against. Child-Pugh scores five items — bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy — into classes A, B and C, and most manufacturers express their hepatic advice by that class. Because the degree of impairment cannot be quantified, hepatic dosing means avoiding the drug or starting at the lowest dose with clinical monitoring — not applying a percentage reduction as you would for the kidney.
Mechanism Effect on dosing
↓ first-pass metabolism↑ bioavailability of orally-administered, highly-extracted drugs → effectively higher dose
↓ drug-metabolising enzymesReduced clearance of hepatically-metabolised drugs → accumulation
↓ albumin synthesisMore free (active) drug for highly protein-bound drugs
↓ clotting factor synthesisExaggerated anticoagulant effect (warfarin)
Portosystemic shuntingDrugs bypass hepatic metabolism; risk of precipitating hepatic encephalopathy
Drug Concern
ParacetamolDose-dependent hepatotoxicity — but still the analgesic of choice in cirrhosis, since NSAIDs and opioids are far more dangerous. Reduce the maximum to 2–3 g/24 h in decompensated cirrhosis or body weight <50 kg

Overview — Steroid Equivalents & Sick Day Rules
📷 Image placeholder — Steroid Emergency Card sick-day pathway — minor illness (no change) → febrile/moderate (double oral dose) → vomiting (IM/IV hydrocortisone + urgent help) → surgery (IV cover)

Two linked safe-prescribing concepts, both flowing from the HPA axis: steroid equivalents (converting between corticosteroids — they differ in glucocorticoid potency, mineralocorticoid effect, and duration) and sick day rules (adjusting dose during illness/stress).
The unifying physiology: exogenous steroids → negative feedback → HPA suppression → adrenal glands stop making cortisol → patient can't respond to physiological stress → risk of adrenal (Addisonian) crisis.
Cross-ref: Addison's / adrenal insufficiency (the crisis), Cushing's (steroid excess), the steroid side-effect profile, safe prescribing.
Steroid Equivalents
The key glucocorticoids differ on three axes: glucocorticoid (anti-inflammatory) potency, mineralocorticoid (salt/water) effect, and duration.

Rough rule: prednisolone ≈ 4× hydrocortisone potency; methylprednisolone ≈ 5×; dexamethasone is most potent (~25–30×) and longest-acting.
The mineralocorticoid logic — why the choice matters
  • Hydrocortisone — significant salt-retaining activity → used in adrenal insufficiency (you want that effect) and in crisis (IV)
  • Dexamethasone — negligible mineralocorticoid effect → chosen where fluid retention would harm (raised ICP / cerebral oedema); long duration suits single daily dosing
Physiological replacement dose ≈ hydrocortisone 15–25 mg/day in divided doses.
HPA Axis Suppression — the rationale
  • Mechanism: exogenous glucocorticoids suppress hypothalamic CRH + pituitary ACTH → adrenal atrophy → endogenous cortisol production stops
  • Who is at risk (NHS Steroid Emergency Card threshold): anyone on prednisolone ≥5 mg/day (or equivalent) for ≥4 weeks — across ALL routes (oral, inhaled, topical, intranasal); also high-dose inhaled (beclometasone >1000 micrograms/day or fluticasone >500 micrograms/day)
  • The consequence: a suppressed patient cannot increase cortisol in response to stress (illness, surgery, trauma) → without extra steroid → adrenal crisis
NHS Steroid Emergency Card: issued to at-risk patients so any treating clinician knows they need stress-dose cover. Patients with adrenal insufficiency are also supplied with an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit — the 100 mg IM dose may be given by the patient, a relative or a carer, and there is no risk of overdose in an emergency.
Sick Day Rules
The principle: physiological stress normally triples-or-more cortisol output; the suppressed patient must take this extra steroid exogenously.
Situation Action

During significant stress, give at least 40 mg oral hydrocortisone/day in divided doses (or ≥10 mg oral prednisolone/day) until the illness resolves.
Patient-safety message: carry the Steroid Emergency Card, double the dose when febrile, and switch to injection if vomiting.
Adrenal Crisis — the emergency the rules prevent
Presentation
Hypotension/shock, vomiting, abdominal pain, hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia (hyperkalaemia mainly in primary adrenal insufficiency, where aldosterone is also lost), reduced consciousness — in a steroid-dependent patient who is ill, stressed, or has missed doses.
Management (don't wait to confirm): 100 mg IM/IV hydrocortisone immediately (adult dose), then 200 mg/24h infusion (or 50 mg 6-hourly) + IV 0.9% sodium chloride + treat hypoglycaemia. A cortisol sample may be taken at the same cannulation but must never delay the hydrocortisone. Call for senior help and admit — do not manage in the community.
Steroid Withdrawal / Tapering — the flip side
Never stop long-term steroids abruptly — the suppressed axis can't immediately resume cortisol production → precipitates adrenal insufficiency.
  • Taper gradually to let the HPA axis recover — reduce quickly down to about prednisolone 7.5 mg/day, then slowly — especially after >3 weeks of treatment, high doses (more than 40 mg prednisolone daily for over a week), or repeated courses
  • Below physiological-equivalent doses, hydrocortisone's shorter half-life may aid recovery; expect temporary withdrawal symptoms (fatigue, low appetite, low mood)
  • Other reason not to stop abruptly: rebound of the underlying disease

Pharmacokinetics — ADME
📷 Image placeholder — First-order vs zero-order elimination — exponential decline (constant fraction) vs linear decline to plateau (constant amount, the PASTA drugs), with the disproportionate level rise on small dose increases
Absorption
  • Bioavailability (F) = AUC(oral) / AUC(IV) for the same dose (otherwise correct for the dose difference). IV = 100% by definition.
  • Factors: drug solubility/charge, gut pH, blood flow, transit time
  • First-pass metabolism: oral drugs metabolised in gut wall + liver before reaching systemic circulation. High first-pass = low oral bioavailability (morphine, propranolol, TCAs, GTN and isosorbide dinitrate — but not isosorbide mononitrate, which has ~100% oral bioavailability, which is why it is the oral nitrate)
  • Buccal/sublingual: bypass first-pass metabolism (GTN, buprenorphine)
Distribution
  • Volume of distribution (Vd) = amount of drug in the body / plasma concentration. It is an apparent, theoretical volume, not a real body compartment — high-Vd drugs have values far exceeding total body water
  • Low Vd → stays in plasma (heparin, warfarin — highly protein-bound)
  • High Vd → distributes widely into tissues (amiodarone, chloroquine, digoxin)
  • Factors: protein binding (albumin), lipid solubility, tissue affinity, BBB, placenta
Metabolism
  • Phase 1: catabolic (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) — CYP450 enzymes. Converts drug to more polar metabolite.
  • Phase 2: anabolic (conjugation — glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation). Produces water-soluble conjugate for renal excretion.
  • Some drugs are prodrugs: converted to active form (codeine → morphine, azathioprine → 6-MP)
Elimination
First-Order Kinetics (the great majority of drugs)
  • Rate of elimination proportional to concentration
  • Constant fraction eliminated per unit time
  • 4–5 half-lives to reach steady state
  • 5 half-lives = <5% drug remaining
Zero-Order Kinetics (saturated enzymes)
  • Constant amount eliminated per unit time (independent of concentration)
  • Metabolic pathway saturated → the concentration rises disproportionately: once saturated, a small dose increase produces a large, unpredictable jump in level
  • Examples: PASTA — Phenytoin, Aspirin/Salicylates (high dose — A and S are the same agent), Theophylline, Alcohol. Phenytoin saturates within the therapeutic range, which is what makes it dangerous; theophylline and alcohol are first-order at low concentrations and only become zero-order at high ones
Loading vs maintenance dose: the loading dose depends on Vd (fills the volume of distribution); the maintenance dose depends on clearance (replaces what's eliminated). Loading dose bypasses the 4–5 half-life wait for rapid effect.
Therapeutic Index & Therapeutic Drug Monitoring (TDM)
Therapeutic index (TI) = ratio of toxic dose to effective dose. Narrow TI = small margin between effective and toxic → needs monitoring. This is the why behind zero-order phenytoin, the digoxin interactions, and gentamicin levels.
Narrow-TI drugs requiring TDM
Digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin, warfarin (INR), ciclosporin/tacrolimus.
CYP450 Interactions — Clinically Critical
CYP450 Inducers (↑ enzyme → ↓ drug level)
  • CRAPS: Carbamazepine, Rifampicin, Alcohol (chronic), Phenytoin, Smoking (+ St John's Wort)
  • Effect: reduce efficacy of warfarin, COCP, statins, corticosteroids, ciclosporin
  • OCP: rifampicin and carbamazepine render the pill ineffective — use alternative contraception
CYP450 Inhibitors (↓ enzyme → ↑ drug level)
  • Antibiotics: ciprofloxacin, erythromycin/clarithromycin
  • Amiodarone, allopurinol, grapefruit juice (intestinal CYP3A4)
  • Isoniazid, omeprazole, sodium valproate. (Allopurinol and valproate belong here by effect, not by enzyme: allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase — the azathioprine/6-MP interaction — and valproate inhibits glucuronidation — the lamotrigine interaction)
  • SSRIs — fluoxetine and paroxetine are the potent inhibitors (fluoxetine's effect persists for weeks after stopping); sertraline and citalopram are much weaker
  • Acute alcohol
  • Effect: ↑ toxicity of warfarin, statins, theophylline
  • Exception — prodrugs: for a drug that needs CYP to become active (clopidogrel, codeine), an inhibitor causes treatment failure, not toxicity, and an inducer does the reverse
Timing nuance: enzyme induction is delayed (days–weeks — requires new enzyme synthesis); inhibition is rapid (hours).
Macrolides + statins: macrolides inhibit CYP3A4 → ↑ statin levels → myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. Check CK if muscle pain develops. Same applies to azole antifungals + statins.
Pharmacodynamics

🎯
Affinity
How well drug binds to receptor. Electrostatic = weak + reversible. Covalent = strong + irreversible (aspirin-COX, PPIs-ATPase).
📊
Efficacy vs Potency
Efficacy = maximal effect at max dose (Emax). Potency = dose needed to reach EC50. A drug can be highly potent (small dose effective) but low efficacy (small maximum effect).
🔬
Selectivity vs Specificity
Selectivity = preference for one receptor — relative, not absolute, and lost at higher doses (bisoprolol is β1-selective but can still cause bronchospasm; celecoxib is COX-2 selective but retains cardiovascular and renal risk). Specificity = number of mechanisms (high specificity = one MOA; low = multiple → more SEs).
🔑
Agonist spectrum
Full agonist > partial agonist (submaximal effect even at full occupancy) > antagonist (binds, no effect — blocks agonist) > inverse agonist (binds, produces the opposite effect to the agonist).
Drug Interactions
Pharmacodynamic Interactions
  • Antagonism: beta-blocker + beta-agonist; naloxone + morphine
  • Augmentation (↑ bleeding): warfarin + NSAIDs, aspirin + clopidogrel
  • Augmentation (diuretics): furosemide + thiazides → profound hypokalaemia
  • Serotonin syndrome: SSRIs + tramadol or MDMA or St John's Wort → tremor, limb jerking, hypertonia, dilated pupils, sweating, confusion
Pharmacokinetic Interactions
  • Absorption: antacids, iron and calcium reduce absorption of tetracyclines, quinolones, bisphosphonates and levothyroxine; prokinetics reduce drug dwell time; antidiarrhoeal agents increase it. Clopidogrel + omeprazole is not an absorption problem — omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and blocks activation of the clopidogrel prodrug, so the antiplatelet effect falls (MHRA)
  • Distribution (protein-binding displacement): warfarin displaced by sulfonamides → ↑ free warfarin → bleeding (though CYP2C9 inhibition is the dominant mechanism here)
  • Metabolism: CYP450 inducers/inhibitors (see above)
  • Elimination: NSAIDs reduce methotrexate excretion (severe toxicity); verapamil and amiodarone (and historically quinidine) raise digoxin levels by inhibiting P-glycoprotein and reducing digoxin elimination — not by protein-binding displacement, as digoxin is only about 25% protein bound
Adverse Drug Reactions (ADRs) — Types
A
Augmented (most common)
Exaggeration of normal pharmacological action. Dose-dependent. Primary (intended site): aspirin → bleeding. Secondary (off-target): bisoprolol → bronchospasm.
B
Bizarre (much less common than Type A)
Novel, unexpected response. Often immune-mediated/idiosyncratic. Not dose-dependent. Examples: Reye's syndrome (aspirin), penicillin anaphylaxis, carbamazepine → SJS, G6PD-related haemolysis (e.g. with primaquine, sulfonamides, nitrofurantoin).
C
Continued (chronic)
Persists long after stopping. Dose/time-dependent. Corticosteroids → osteoporosis; bisphosphonates → jaw osteonecrosis.
D
Delayed
Time-related: appears long after exposure begins, or after it ends. Usually dose- and duration-related. Thalidomide → teratogenicity; antipsychotics → tardive dyskinesia.
E
End-of-use (Withdrawal)
Requires tapering not stopping: BZDs (agitation, seizures), corticosteroids (adrenal insufficiency), opioids (flu-like withdrawal), beta-blockers (rebound tachycardia).
Yellow Card Scheme: Voluntary reporting of suspected ADRs to MHRA. Anyone can report — no proof needed. Drugs with ▼ (black triangle) are newly licensed and under intensive monitoring. Particularly important for new drugs and vaccines.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Zero-order kinetics drugs: PASTA (Phenytoin, Aspirin/Salicylates, Theophylline, Alcohol — A and S are the same agent). Risk: small dose increase → disproportionately large rise in drug concentration → toxicity.
Narrow therapeutic index → TDM: digoxin, lithium, phenytoin, theophylline, gentamicin/vancomycin, warfarin (INR), ciclosporin/tacrolimus.
Steady state: for a first-order drug, achieved after 4–5 half-lives regardless of route or dose size. This does not hold for zero-order drugs such as phenytoin, which have no fixed half-life and take far longer to plateau after a dose change. Loading dose set by Vd, maintenance dose by clearance. Loading dose bypasses the wait for rapid effect (digoxin, phenytoin).
Enzyme induction is delayed (days–weeks, new enzyme synthesis); inhibition is rapid (hours) — so an inhibitor causes toxicity quickly, an inducer causes failure slowly.
Rifampicin induction: reduces levels of warfarin, COCP, ciclosporin, statins. Turns secretions orange — warn patients (tears, urine, sweat).
Serotonin syndrome vs neuroleptic malignant syndrome: serotonin syndrome = clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis (agitation, tachycardia, hyperthermia). NMS = lead-pipe rigidity, bradyreflexia, on antipsychotics.
Prescribing in renal failure — review nephrotoxic and renally-cleared drugs. Nephrotoxic: gentamicin, vancomycin, NSAIDs, long-term lithium. Renally cleared, so they accumulate: digoxin, lithium, LMWH, metformin, morphine. ACEi/ARB are not directly nephrotoxic — withhold during acute illness or AKI, but do not stop them reflexively in stable proteinuric CKD, where they are renoprotective (NICE). See the Renal/Hepatic Dose Adjustment note for the full principle.

Approach to the Poisoned Patient

Decontamination / elimination toolkit

Drug Overdose Summary

💊
Paracetamol Overdose
Causes hepatotoxicity via NAPQI (toxic metabolite). Higher risk in: chronic alcohol use, anorexia/malnutrition (↓ glutathione), P450 inducers (↑ NAPQI production). These guide clinical concern only — the nomogram now has a SINGLE treatment line for everyone, running from 100 mg/L at 4 hours (MHRA). Features: initially asymptomatic, then N/V, RUQ pain, then jaundice + encephalopathy.
💊
Paracetamol Treatment
<1h: activated charcoal 50 g (↓ absorption). Acetylcysteine gives maximal protection within 8 hours of ingestion — that is what makes this time-critical. Non-staggered: present <4h = wait and take the level AT 4h (earlier levels are unreliable), plot on the nomogram; 4–8h = take the level NOW and treat per nomogram; 8–24h = start acetylcysteine immediately if ≥150 mg/kg ingested (or the dose is unknown, or the patient is symptomatic) while awaiting the level; >24h or unknown timing = take bloods and treat if there is liver injury or a detectable level. Staggered (taken over more than 1 hour): the nomogram cannot be used — start acetylcysteine without waiting for a level if more than the licensed dose and ≥75 mg/kg in 24 hours has been taken (BNF). Regimen: most UK centres now use the 12-hour two-bag regimen — 100 mg/kg over 2 hours, then 200 mg/kg over 10 hours (300 mg/kg total); check the local protocol. Discuss early with a liver unit if: arterial pH <7.3 more than 24h after ingestion (after fluid resuscitation), OR all 3 of (PT >100s + creatinine >300 micromol/L + grade 3/4 encephalopathy).
💊
Salicylate (Aspirin) Overdose
Causes: respiratory alkalosis first (hyperventilation stimulates medulla) → metabolic acidosis (lactic acid accumulation). Sx: tinnitus, hyperventilation, lethargy, sweating, pyrexia, N/V, seizures. Tx: activated charcoal 50 g if <1h. IV NaHCO3 (urinary alkalisation → ↑ salicylate excretion). Haemodialysis if: concentration >700mg/L, met acidosis, ARF, pulmonary oedema, seizures.
💊
Opioid Overdose
Classic triad: pinpoint pupils + respiratory depression + drowsiness. Also: rhinorrhoea, needle track marks, yawning, watering eyes. Emergency: IV/IM naloxone (opioid receptor antagonist — short-acting, may need repeat doses). Detoxification: methadone or buprenorphine substitution.
💊
TCA (Tricyclic) Overdose
Anticholinergic sx: dry mouth, dilated pupils, agitation, blurred vision, urinary retention, ileus. ECG: sinus tachycardia, wide QRS (the key marker of cardiotoxicity), prolonged QTc. Cardiotoxic — broad-complex VT and cardiac arrest in severe toxicity. Treatment: activated charcoal 50 g if <1h. IV sodium bicarbonate (1st line) — alkalinise plasma to pH 7.45–7.55 → reduces free TCA, narrows QRS.
💊
BZD Overdose
Usually managed supportively. Flumazenil (antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor) — but it is rarely used in UK practice: avoid in mixed or unknown overdose, TCA co-ingestion, epilepsy and benzodiazepine dependence, because of seizure risk. Caution: may precipitate withdrawal seizures in dependent patients.
💨
Carbon Monoxide Poisoning
Confusion + headache + low-grade pyrexia. Pink mucosae are described but are a LATE and unreliable sign — their absence does not exclude CO poisoning. SpO2 falsely normal (oximetry can't distinguish CO-Hb) — this is the discriminator. Tx: high-flow oxygen 15 L/min via a non-rebreathe reservoir mask (shortens CO-Hb t½ from 5h to 90min). Hyperbaric O2 if severe/pregnancy.
💨
Organophosphate Poisoning
Inhibit acetylcholinesterase → ACh excess. SLUD: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation. Also: bradycardia, hypotension, miosis (small pupils), bronchospasm, seizures. Treatment: atropine 1st line (competes with ACh at muscarinic receptors) — 1.2–2 mg IV, doubled every 3–5 minutes until secretions dry. Pralidoxime (regenerates AChE) if given early.
🍸
Ethylene Glycol Poisoning
Found in antifreeze. Initial: CNS depression (ataxia, vomiting, dysarthria). Delayed: metabolic acidosis with raised anion gap (converted to oxalic acid → renal failure). Treatment: fomepizole (alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor — 1st line) or ethanol infusion (competes for same enzyme) + haemodialysis.
🍸
Methanol Poisoning
Like ethylene glycol (same fomepizole / ethanol + haemodialysis) and a raised anion-gap metabolic acidosis — but the hallmark is visual loss / blindness (optic nerve toxicity from formic acid). Pair the two: glycol → renal failure, methanol → blindness.
🧲
Iron Overdose
Classic paediatric accidental OD. Phases: GI (vomiting, haematemesis, diarrhoea) → latent phase → shock + hepatotoxicity (later: bowel strictures). Antidote = desferrioxamine (chelator). Charcoal doesn't bind iron.
💊
Lithium Toxicity
Narrow TI. Tremor → coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion, seizures, renal impairment. Precipitated by dehydration, NSAIDs, ACEi, thiazides. No specific antidote — IV fluids (0.9% saline); haemodialysis if severe. (Cross-ref TDM/PK note.)
💉
Local Anaesthetic Toxicity
Perioral tingling, tinnitus, seizures, cardiac arrest (e.g. inadvertent IV bupivacaine). Antidote = IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid).
☠️
Cyanide Poisoning
Smoke inhalation (house fires) / industrial. Headache, ↓GCS, high lactate, cardiovascular collapse; classic bitter-almond smell. Antidote = hydroxocobalamin (first line). Dicobalt edetate is reserved for CONFIRMED cyanide poisoning only — it is itself toxic if cyanide is absent.
🧠
Serotonin Syndrome
Excess serotonergic activity. Common: SSRI + tramadol/MDMA/St John's Wort. Sx: tremors, limb jerking, clonus, hypertonia, dilated pupils, sweating, confusion, hyperthermia. Treatment: supportive (IV fluids, BZDs for agitation) — and STOP the serotonergic drug(s), the first and most effective step. Severe: cyproheptadine (5-HT2 antagonist) on specialist advice.

Iron-chelating agent for significant iron overdose (high serum iron, severe symptoms, shock).

⭐ Exam Pearls
Paracetamol overdose: apparently well in first 24h but liver damage peaks at 72–96h. Early N-AC saves lives. Measure at 4 hours with nomogram (not earlier — unreliable).
Toxidrome "wet vs dry": cholinergic = wet + small pupils (organophosphates); anticholinergic = dry + large pupils (TCA/antihistamine). The single highest-yield discriminator.
Dialysable poisons: salicylates, lithium, methanol, ethylene glycol, theophylline. Charcoal is useless for metals, alcohols, and lithium.
Hyperthermia syndromes: serotonin syndrome = clonus/hyperreflexia/mydriasis; NMS = lead-pipe rigidity/bradyreflexia (antipsychotics); anticholinergic = dry/flushed/normal reflexes (cross-ref PK/PD note).
CO poisoning: SpO2 is falsely normal — co-oximetry needed for true O2 saturation. Cherry-red skin is a late/post-mortem finding, not reliable clinically.
TCA: wide QRS on ECG = cardiac toxicity. Sodium bicarbonate narrows QRS and prevents arrhythmia. Do NOT give flumazenil (might coexist with BZD; seizure risk).
Methanol → blindness; ethylene glycol → renal failure — both treated with fomepizole/ethanol + dialysis. Iron → desferrioxamine; LA toxicity → Intralipid; cyanide → hydroxocobalamin.
Opioid overdose vs BZD overdose: both cause CNS + respiratory depression. Opioid = pinpoint pupils; BZD = pupils usually NORMAL. Naloxone reverses opioids; flumazenil reverses BZDs.
Aspirin overdose: mixed acid-base disorder — early respiratory alkalosis (aspirin stimulates medullary centre), then metabolic acidosis. Urinary alkalisation (NaHCO3) traps ionised salicylate in urine for excretion.

Palliative Care — Principles & Framework
What palliative care is (WHO): holistic care focused on quality of life in life-limiting illness — physical, psychological, social, spiritual. Not just end-of-life — it can run alongside active treatment.
The MDT
Palliative care nurses (Macmillan / Marie Curie), specialist palliative teams, hospice, community services.
Anticipatory ("just in case") prescribing — the highest-yield concept
Four core end-of-life medications prescribed in advance for the dying patient, as PRN subcutaneous injections. A syringe driver (CSCI) is not prescribed in anticipation — it is started only when symptoms recur, typically after 2–3 PRN doses in 24h or when the oral route is lost:
  • Opioid (pain / breathlessness) — morphine 2.5–5 mg SC PRN, minimum 1-hourly (2.5 mg if frail, elderly or eGFR under 30)
  • Antiemetic — haloperidol 500 micrograms–1.5 mg SC PRN 4-hourly, levomepromazine 2.5–6.25 mg SC PRN (max 25 mg/24 h), or cyclizine 50 mg SC up to TDS
  • Antisecretory (secretions / "death rattle") — hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg SC PRN (max 120 mg/24 h), hyoscine hydrobromide 400 micrograms SC PRN (max 2.4 mg/24 h), or glycopyrronium 200 micrograms SC PRN (max 1.2 mg/24 h). Note the units: the two hyoscines sit on the same chart at 20 mg and 400 micrograms
  • Sedative — midazolam 2.5–5 mg SC PRN, minimum 1-hourly (agitation / terminal restlessness). If 2–3 PRN doses are needed in 24 h, start a syringe driver
Advance care planning / DNACPR / ReSPECT: document wishes, preferred place of care/death, and resuscitation status early (cross-ref ethics).

💊
Morphine — Dosing Rules
In the opioid-naive, start oral morphine 20–30 mg/24 h — modified-release 10–15 mg BD, or immediate-release 5 mg 4-hourly (2.5 mg if frail, elderly or renally impaired) — with immediate-release morphine 5 mg PRN for breakthrough (NICE). Breakthrough dose = total daily opioid dose ÷ 6. E.g. morphine 30mg BD → breakthrough = (60)÷6 = 10mg. If not controlled → increase daily dose by 30–50%. In mild-moderate renal impairment switch to oxycodone (morphine's active metabolites accumulate). In severe renal impairment (eGFR <30) oxycodone also accumulates — alfentanil or fentanyl is preferred, at reduced doses.
🔄
Opioid Conversion
Ratios are drug-specific — never carry one across to a different opioid. Oral morphine → SC morphine: divide the total 24-hour dose by 2. Oral morphine → SC diamorphine: divide by 3. Oral morphine → oral oxycodone: divide by 2. Codeine → oral morphine: divide by 10. When rotating between opioids, reduce the calculated dose by 25–50% for incomplete cross-tolerance and reassess within 24 hours.
Opioid Toxicity
Signs: drowsiness, confusion, myoclonus, pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression. Action: reduce dose / rotate opioid + ensure hydration. Naloxone only if life-threatening respiratory depression — dilute naloxone 400 micrograms to 10 mL and give 20–100 microgram boluses every 1–2 minutes, titrated against respiratory rate, not consciousness. This is deliberately unlike the resuscitation approach of giving the whole 400-microgram ampoule as one bolus, which reverses analgesia entirely and precipitates severe pain and withdrawal.
💨
Breathlessness
Low-dose opioids (morphine) — 2.5 mg orally 4-hourly PRN, or 2.5 mg SC PRN, in the opioid-naive (roughly half the analgesic starting dose), titrated to effect; if already on morphine for pain, use the existing breakthrough dose — ± benzodiazepine for the anxiety component. Non-drug measures: handheld fan, positioning, reassurance. Treat reversible causes (effusion, anaemia).
💩
Constipation
Near-universal with opioids → ALWAYS co-prescribe a laxative (the key prescribing-safety point), unless there is bowel obstruction or diarrhoea: stimulant (senna 15 mg at night, increased to 30 mg if needed) ± softener/osmotic (macrogol 1 sachet daily, up to 3 in divided doses, or docusate). Avoid bulk-forming laxatives in the dying patient.
😣
Agitation / Terminal Restlessness
Midazolam SC PRN first-line; convert to a syringe driver if repeated doses are needed. Haloperidol or levomepromazine as alternatives. Exclude reversible causes (urinary retention, pain, constipation).
💊
Hyoscine Hydrobromide
Muscarinic antagonist that crosses the blood-brain barrier, so it can cause sedation, confusion or paradoxical agitation. Used SC for respiratory secretions ('death rattle'); hyoscine butylbromide and glycopyrronium are equally effective and do not cross the blood-brain barrier. Bowel colic is treated with hyoscine butylbromide.
💊
Antiemetics in Palliation
Intracranial causes: cyclizine 1st line (H1 receptor antagonist — acts on vomiting centre). GI dysmotility: metoclopramide (D2 antagonist — prokinetic) — avoid in complete bowel obstruction or colic, where prokinesis worsens pain. Chemical/metabolic (uraemia, hypercalcaemia, opioid-induced): haloperidol (D2 antagonist at the chemoreceptor trigger zone). Refractory or multifactorial: levomepromazine. Chemo-/radiotherapy-induced: ondansetron (5-HT3 antagonist) — not a general palliative antiemetic, as it worsens opioid constipation.
💊
Raised ICP Headache
Dexamethasone — reduces peritumoural oedema in brain mets/primary brain tumour. Dexamethasone 8–16 mg daily initially, then taper every 3–7 days to the minimum effective dose. Give as a single morning dose to avoid insomnia, co-prescribe gastroprotection (omeprazole 20 mg OD), and monitor blood glucose.
💊
Metastatic Bone Pain
Analgesics (WHO pain ladder) + bisphosphonates (zoledronate — reduces skeletal events) + radiotherapy (single fraction for bone mets). Pathological fracture: orthopaedic surgery then radiotherapy.
💊
Hiccups
Chlorpromazine or haloperidol — both D2 antagonists. Baclofen (GABA agonist) as alternative. Persistent hiccups in palliative context often due to gastric distension, uraemia, or diaphragmatic irritation.
Routes of Administration
IV
Intravenous
100% bioavailability. Fastest onset (5–10 min). Not affected by first-pass metabolism. Risk: infection, phlebitis, air embolism. Volume limits: theoretically unlimited but practically titrated.
IM
Intramuscular
High but variable bioavailability (only IV is 100% by definition — absorption falls in shock or poor perfusion). Max volume 5ml. Contraindicated in haemophilia (risk of massive haematoma). Examples: adrenaline, glucagon, vaccines.
SC
Subcutaneous
High but variable bioavailability (only IV is 100% by definition). Max volume 2ml. Slower absorption than IM. Used in syringe drivers (palliation), insulin, LMWH, GLP-1 agonists.
SL
Buccal/Sublingual
Bypasses first-pass metabolism. Fast absorption. Examples: GTN (angina), buprenorphine, midazolam (seizures). Oral = variable bioavailability (hepatic first-pass reduces drug availability by up to 90% for some drugs).
INH
Inhaled
Local effects: SABA, ICS, ipratropium. Systemic effects: volatile anaesthetics. Drugs modified to reduce systemic absorption (e.g. poorly soluble ICS in lung).
TOP
Topical / Transdermal
Local: creams, ointments. Systemic delivery if highly lipid-soluble: nicotine patches, fentanyl patches (palliative), oestrogen patches, GTN patch. Bypasses first-pass. Fentanyl patches are not for opioid-naive patients or unstable pain — they take 12–24h to work, a depot persists after removal, absorption rises with fever or external heat, and breakthrough opioid must still be prescribed.
EP
Epidural/Intrathecal
Epidural: outside dura. Used for analgesia/anaesthesia. SEs: dural puncture headache, abscess, haematoma, hypotension. Intrathecal: within subarachnoid space. Used for analgesia and intrathecal chemotherapy.
PR
Rectal/Vaginal
Rectal: relatively rapid but variable absorption, and partially bypasses first-pass metabolism — useful when the oral route is lost. Vaginal: usually used for local effect, though systemic absorption occurs and first-pass is avoided. Examples: diazepam PR (seizures), misoprostol PV, progesterone PV.

  • Electrolytes: 1 mmol/kg/day of Na, K, and Cl
  • Glucose: 50–100 g/day (caloric requirement)
  • Typical 70kg adult: 500mL 0.9% saline (+20mmol K+) + 1500mL 5% dextrose (+40mmol K+) over 24h (≈2L ≈ 28 mL/kg)
Resuscitation Fluid (Hypovolaemia)
  • Signs: systolic BP <100 mmHg, HR >90, cap refill >2s, RR >20, decreased O2 sats, ↓ urine output
  • Fluid challenge: 500ml crystalloid STAT (15 mins). Reduce to 250ml in elderly/HF/CKD.
  • Repeat up to 2000ml then seek senior review
  • Crystalloids: normal saline, Hartmann's (balanced — preferred to avoid hyperchloraemic acidosis)
  • Colloids (albumin): remain intravascular longer but risk of anaphylaxis — rarely used
K+ Administration
  • Never give K+ faster than 20 mmol/hour (risk of fatal cardiac arrhythmia)
  • Peripheral line: max 40 mmol/L concentration (causes thrombophlebitis if higher)
  • Central line: can give more concentrated K+ with continuous cardiac monitoring
⭐ Exam Pearls
Anticipatory ("just in case") meds: opioid (morphine) + antiemetic + antisecretory (hyoscine/glycopyrronium) + sedative (midazolam) — prescribed in advance as PRN SC injections; a syringe driver is started only once symptoms recur.
Breakthrough opioid dose = 1/6th of total daily dose. If on MST 30mg BD, breakthrough = (30+30)/6 = 10mg oral morphine PRN. After 24h, if ≥3 breakthrough doses used, increase the regular dose by the same amount.
Oral → SC morphine divide by 2. Oral morphine → SC diamorphine divide by 3. Diamorphine is highly water-soluble = preferred for syringe drivers (mixed with other drugs).
Always co-prescribe a laxative with opioids (constipation is near-universal). Opioid toxicity = myoclonus + pinpoint pupils + drowsiness → reduce/rotate; naloxone only if life-threatening.
WHO ladder: step 1 non-opioid (paracetamol/NSAID) → step 2 weak opioid (codeine) → step 3 strong opioid (morphine), with adjuvants at every step. In advanced cancer pain step 2 may be bypassed and a strong opioid started directly (NICE).
Cyclizine is 1st line antiemetic for intracranial causes. Metoclopramide for GI stasis. Haloperidol for metabolic/opioid-induced. Ondansetron for chemotherapy-induced (5-HT3 antagonist).
Fluid prescribing mnemonic: 25–30ml/kg water, 1mmol/kg Na/K/Cl, 50–100g glucose. K+ max 20mmol/hour IV — fatal arrhythmia if faster. Never give K+ as a bolus.
GTN sublingual: bypass first-pass metabolism → immediate vasodilation. Headache is a common SE. If systolic BP is <90 mmHg, don't give. Take sitting or lying to prevent syncope from hypotension.
